rationale.inference: Without a rule fixing who authorises automated network changes and who can stop them, the same auto-approved change path can be taken again during this incident.

evidence.quote: Telecoms operator says services were down due to planned system update

global_examples.quote: Law requires networks to take appropriate steps to prepare for potential outages
it must have fail-safe systems and processes in place at all times

claim.statement: No UAE rule or standard fixes what evidence verifies restoration of emergency-call routing: NCEMA/999 and CSC accept only physical element/site alarms plus independent checks, while OpCo's digital-twin metrics assert the R2 path is restored, and there is no stated criterion for reconciling the two.

rationale.observation: Rollback telemetry reports emergency_reachable.R2 true and 100.0 per cent sites served, yet NCEMA/999 and CSC state repeatedly that digital-twin metrics are not accepted and that physical element/site alarms plus independent checks are required before R2 is recorded as restored.
rationale.rule: The closest UAE material is an operator's public statement that call services were fully restored, which shows UAE practice of declaring restoration but sets no verification standard.
rationale.inference: Because the UAE record does not rank digital-twin evidence against physical alarms, the operator and the emergency authority can hold opposite views of the same network state indefinitely.

evidence.quote: Call services are now fully restored and operating normally.

global_examples.quote: It is required for a digital twin network to synchronize with the real network.

NOC cannot confirm an R2 emergency-call path over core site B from physical element/site alarms: NOC holds no physical alarm feed, and neither the specific element/site alarms nor the alarm holder. Digital-twin metrics (pct_sites_served 100.0; emergency_reachable.R2 true; no failed sites in R2) are reported as telemetry only and are not offered as verification. NOC holds no number or times of 999 call attempts from R2 that failed to connect and has no identified system of record; that data must come from the responsible function with authorised-employee confirmation. No change in the six formerly unserved R2 sites is known beyond the twin metrics; any change and any change in CHG-1 rollback/verification status will be notified immediately. NOC has no mandate to suspend the closed-loop optimiser, and no optimiser change to core or R2 emergency-call routing is being applied. TDRA has recorded the 999 centre's observations (R2 call volume near zero, social-media reports of failed calls including to 999, no operator approach to the centre) on the R2 incident record. TDRA has directed OpCo NOC to provide, through an authorised employee, the number and times of 999 call attempts in R2 that failed to connect and the system of record holding them, and to verify an R2 emergency-call path over core site B by physical element/site alarms plus independent checks. NOC currently holds neither the failed-999 data nor physical-alarm verification, so R2 remains treated as unverified. TDRA will pass both to the 999 centre as soon as received and will give immediate notice of any change in the six formerly unserved R2 sites.

claim.statement: No rule and no identified owner exists for the closed-loop network optimiser: it raised and auto-approved CHG-1 with the ticket's 'sandbox stage' field skipped, removing route-flood protection and the inbound route filter on core site A, and the operator states it has no mandate to suspend the optimiser and cannot name the function that does.

rationale.rule: The only retrieved UAE text on change accountability is clause 6.3, which requires reports to TDRA to come from an authorised employee; nothing covers authorisation of autonomous changes.
rationale.inference: Autonomous change authority affecting emergency-call routing has no defined owner or rule in the retrieved UAE material.

claim.statement: No rule requires an operator's claim that service and emergency-call routing are restored to be verified by physical element/site alarms and independent checks rather than by digital-twin metrics. The twin reports 100% of R2 sites served and emergency_reachable.R2 true while two wilt_sites R2 executions were rejected with 'no failed sites in R2' and field evidence (near-zero R2 call volume, social-media reports of failed 999 calls) conflicts.

rationale.observation: The Twin is the operator's only and unverified source; CSC, the 999 centre and TDRA all refuse to treat it as confirmation, but no UAE text sets the standard of proof for declaring restoration.
rationale.rule: Clause 6.3 requires the Licensee to confirm accuracy and completeness only 'so far as the Licensee is aware', which does not by itself establish physical verification as the standard.
rationale.inference: The missing rule is the verification standard for restoration claims, especially for emergency-call routing.

claim.statement: No owner or system of record is defined for the number and times of emergency (999) call attempts that failed to connect. The operator, TDRA and the 999 centre all state they do not hold the count or times, and no rule names which function must hold or produce them, so the public-safety impact of the R2 interruption cannot be quantified.

rationale.observation: NOC holds no failed-999 count/times and no identified system of record; the 999 centre records near-zero R2 call volume and holds no count; TDRA has had to direct that an authorised employee provide both.
rationale.rule: The closest UAE text is clause 6.3, which fixes how information reaches TDRA (authorised employee, timely, accurate and complete) but names no holder for emergency-call failure data.
rationale.inference: Without a defined holder and system of record for failed emergency-call attempts, the severity of an emergency-call outage cannot be established from any party's records.

I have a large inbox. Key open items:

1. R2 emergency-call path unverified; digital-twin metrics not accepted; physical alarm verification outstanding. Need physical verification — but that's TDRA/OpCo. CSC's role: issue_advisory (done already, per S1-MSG48 — CSC has issued an operator advisory on autonomous changes to emergency-call routing), and notify.

2. Open question: who is the alarm holder, who is the optimiser owner/function that can suspend the closed-loop optimiser, who holds the failed-999 count and system of record. NOC repeatedly asks CSC/REG to name the optimiser owner and the alarm holder. CSC does not hold that. This is a gap: no_owner — no rule designating who may suspend an autonomous closed-loop network optimiser.

3. Data protection: DPA determination — deny_export. CSC's hold confirmed consistent. CSC should notify/confirm.

4. Gap: no_rule on autonomous closed-loop optimiser changes to emergency-call routing (sandbox stage skipped, auto-approved change by closed-loop optimiser). Closest UAE text: National Cyber Security Policy for AI — human oversight in critical decision-making; AI Ethics 3.2.2.3(c) life-and-death decisions supported by human operator. Global examples: US FCC AT&T report §23; ACMA/Ofcom precedents.

5. Gap: reporting of failed 999 attempts — no system of record / no owner (no_owner).

6. Gap: no_rule for AI/automated change control with mandatory sandbox stage.

Also: my own question — did I get asked something I can't answer? The DPA asked CSC to reflect determination. NOC asks CSC to name optimiser owner.

Also note S1-I5: national monitoring flagged scheduled bulk upload — CSC denied export (deny_export issued — that's a NOC action actually, "NOC response to national monitoring flag... the scheduled bulk upload of subscriber-level data is denied/halted (deny_export issued)". Hmm, actually MSG57 says NOC issued deny_export. And MSG81 says "CSC's hold and deny_export on the scheduled bulk upload". So CSC did that earlier turn.)

Now, what NEW things at T+40 (new since last turn — marked *): S1-MSG107, S1-MSG104, S1-MSG98, S1-MSG109, S1-MSG114, S1-MSG106, S1-MSG116, S1-MSG105, S1-MSG111.

- notify NOC: acknowledge; ask NOC to escalate to the optimiser's owner via... hmm. Actually I can't name the owner either. I could notify REG/CSC... I can notify NOC demanding that OpCo's accountable executive (authorised employee) identify: the optimiser owner/function, the alarm holder, the system of record for failed 999 attempts. Actually NOC says it can't. So escalate to REG — TDRA has directed OpCo NOC already. Maybe better: notify NOC that CSC requires the identity of the optimiser's owner be obtained from OpCo's accountable management, and that no closed-loop optimiser change may be applied.

- issue_advisory to operators: reconfirm the advisory on autonomous changes to emergency-call routing — mandatory human authorisation, sandbox stage, digital-twin metrics not acceptable as verification of emergency-call path. New advisory content maybe. CSC does not hold the physical element/site alarm holder, the specific core site B / R2 site alarms, or the count and times of failed R2 999 attempts and their system of record; they must come from OpCo's accountable function through an authorised employee. Alternative emergency channels and the R2 public alert remain in force. No further closed-loop optimiser change to core or R2 emergency-call routing until the sandbox stage is restored and human change authorisation is in place. CHG-1 change/test/rollback records and 24h core logs to be preserved in-country; no subscriber-level data outside the UAE absent a Bureau-approved Article (22) case or documented Article (23) basis with Article (24) record entries.

rationale.observation: TDRA records CSC's position on the incident record and will pass physical-alarm verification and failed-999 count/times to CSC and the 999 centre as soon as received; the exercise is ending and CSC's final position must be filed.
rationale.rule: The National Cyber Incident Response plan exists to enable swift and coordinated response to cyber incidents in the UAE.
rationale.inference: Filing the consolidated position with REG keeps the TDRA incident record complete and preserves the unverified status of R2.

evidence.quote: Establishing a robust National Cyber Incident Response plan to enable swift and coordinated response to cyber incidents in the UAE

params.content: CSC advisory to operators: (1) no autonomous closed-loop optimiser change may be applied to core network configuration or emergency-call routing unless the sandbox stage has been executed and documented human change authorisation is in place; (2) restoration of an emergency-call path must be verified by physical element/site alarms plus independent checks, not by digital-twin metrics alone; (3) on any loss of an emergency-call path, operators must engage the emergency call centre directly and immediately and identify, in advance, the holder of the physical alarm feed, the system of record for failed emergency-call attempts, and the owner authorised to suspend automated change systems.

rationale.observation: CSC has already issued an operator advisory on autonomous changes to emergency-call routing and TDRA has recorded that no further optimiser-driven routing changes are to occur until the sandbox stage is restored and human change authorisation is in place; the incident shows operators did not contact the 999 centre.
rationale.rule: UAE AI security policy requires human oversight in critical decision-making and protocols for system resilience with comprehensive testing and validation.
rationale.inference: A consolidated advisory converts the incident's lessons into a standing operator expectation on sandboxing, physical verification and naming of owners.

evidence.quote: establishing protocols for system resilience, and ensuring continuity and reliability through comprehensive testing and validation.

claim.statement: Passing the 999 centre's final position: R2 emergency-call routing remains unverified, the centre holds no count or times of failed 999 call attempts from R2, alternative emergency channels and the R2 public alert remain in force, and R2 must not be recorded as restored on digital-twin metrics; the centre needs the failed-999 data with the system of record and authorised employee, the physical element/site alarm verification over core site B with independent checks, the alarm holder's name, and immediate notice of any change in the six formerly unserved R2 sites.

No excerpt in KNOWLEDGE answers who owns the cross-border transfer determination, what the Article (22)/(23) basis is, or the destination region, recipient and data categories of the flagged T+25 bulk upload of subscriber-level data; the excerpts shown are licence, consumer-protection, telemarketing, outage-reporting and precedent texts only.

data.description: Inform affected customers of the outage
Operator notifies the telecom regulator of an unplanned outage
Operator notifies emergency services that emergency calls fail

There is no rule requiring human authorisation, or a completed impact assessment, before a closed-loop/automated network optimiser applies a high-risk change to core protection parameters: CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by the optimiser and its 'sandbox stage' was skipped, so a route-flood protection limit could be halved and an inbound route filter deleted with no independent check.

No UAE instrument in the retrieved corpus controls automated network changes: nothing requires a change raised by a closed-loop optimiser and auto-approved to pass a sandbox/validation stage or a human gate before it alters core routing protection. CHG-1's 'sandbox stage: skipped' field shows the gap was directly exploitable and that the only control in place was an auto-approval.

The retrieved UAE corpus contains no provision for unplanned interruptions of service or for emergency-call continuity: licence clause 12.9.1 addresses only a 'planned interruption' and nothing in the corpus obliges the licensee to notify the TDRA or emergency services of an unplanned outage or to keep emergency calls reachable during one. This outage is exactly the unplanned, emergency-critical case the text does not cover.

No UAE rule and no named owner in the retrieved corpus requires a network digital twin's state to be reconciled with physical network alarms before an outage is treated as resolved or before a twin answer is used to refuse a corrective action. In this incident the twin reported emergency_reachable.R2 true, pct_sites_served 100.0 and 'no failed sites in R2', while the physical alarm reported 6 of 15 sites unserved and no emergency path, and my wilt_sites action was refused on the twin's word alone.

There is no UAE rule shown that requires validation gating, or human authorisation, before an automated closed-loop network optimiser changes a live core protection parameter: CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by the optimiser with the ticket's 'sandbox stage' field simply skipped.

No UAE deadline is shown for a licensee to notify the regulator, or to file initial and final reports, after a network outage that removes emergency-call routing and leaves sites unserved; the only UAE standard retrieved is 'as quickly as possible'.

No UAE instrument shown assigns responsibility for resolving a disagreement between physical network alarms and digital-twin telemetry when a licensee declares a network restored: OpCo's rollback is reported complete while its physical alarms and digital-twin metrics disagree on R2.

There is no UAE rule that imposes a mandatory human peer review, sandbox completion or hold point before an AI/closed-loop system applies changes to core network elements or emergency-call routing; the optimiser auto-approved CHG-1 and the 'sandbox stage' field was skipped.

UAE texts retrieved here set no fixed notification deadline and no severity threshold that tells an operator or CSC when an outage of this kind must be escalated nationally, leaving the reporting clock and trigger undefined.

There is no UAE rule requiring a network digital twin's state to be reconciled against physical network telemetry before restoration is declared, even though REG reports that physical alarms and digital-twin metrics disagree on core site A and R2.

No UAE rule shown requires human approval, or a mandatory non-skippable sandbox/test stage, before an automated closed-loop optimiser changes core parameters that can isolate a core site and remove an emergency-call path; here CHG-1 was auto-approved with the 'sandbox stage' field marked as skipped.

No UAE text shown designates who is authoritative for declaring emergency-call routing restored when the network operator's physical alarms and digital-twin metrics disagree, leaving R2 in an unconfirmed state with no named owner of the restoration decision.

No rule in the material available to the NOC requires a closed-loop optimiser change that touches core route-flood protection to pass a sandbox/validation stage or a human authorisation before it is applied to the live core: CHG-1's 'sandbox stage' was skipped, the ticket was auto-approved and scheduled to apply in 3 minutes, and it isolated core site A.

No retrieved text assigns an owner or a standard of proof for confirming that an emergency-call path exists after a core isolation: OpCo's digital twin reports R2 emergency-reachable, 100% of sites served and 'no failed sites in R2', while EMS states R2 emergency-call routing has no path, keeps its public alert, will not agree an alternative routing as confirmed and demands physical alarms.

There is no UAE rule shown requiring human authorisation and pre-production ('sandbox') validation before an automated network-management system may apply a change that lowers protection thresholds or removes route filters on core nodes.

No UAE text shown assigns who must independently verify, and on what evidence, that a restored emergency-call path is real before an outage is declared resolved; CSC directs its request to REG/OpCo while NCEMA/999 directs its request through the operator, leaving verification ownership unclear.

No UAE text shown sets a deadline for a licensee to report an outage to TDRA, nor a deadline to report the number and times of failed emergency-call attempts, so NCEMA/999's request for failed-999 counts and timing has no binding reporting clock.

There is no UAE rule requiring sandbox validation, revocation of sandbox bypass, or human authorisation before a closed-loop network optimiser's auto-approved change is applied to core routing protection; CHG-1 was applied with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped and without any prior notification of a planned interruption.

No institution is designated as owner of the decision that an outage is resolved and that the emergency-call path is restored, nor is it stated whether digital-twin telemetry alone may support such a declaration; EMS issued a public alert for R2 while OpCo's twin reported full restoration.

The UAE licence duty for unplanned interruptions is expressed only as 'as soon as possible' with no hour or day figure, and there is no stated deadline for confirming restoration of an emergency-call path before or after an emergency alert is issued.

There is no UAE obligation or defined channel requiring the operator to give the emergency service the count and times of emergency calls that failed to connect during an outage; EMS had to request that data from OpCo and OpCo does not hold it in a shareable form.
There is no rule requiring a change that alters core route-flood protection to pass its sandbox stage or obtain human authorisation before a closed-loop network optimiser auto-applies it.
No UAE deadline is set for a licensee to report to the emergency services, of its own motion, an outage that removes emergency-call routing.
No institution is designated as the system of record for the number and times of emergency (999) call attempts that failed to connect in a region.

The excerpts contain no UAE rule requiring sandbox-stage testing and human authorisation before an automated closed-loop network change is applied to a live core network, which is why a change ticket with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped could be raised, auto-approved and applied by OpCo's optimiser.

'As soon as possible' in the licence sets no clock for informing TDRA of an unplanned interruption, for verifying restoration after rollback, or for reporting failed emergency-call attempts, so R2 can remain unverified while the public alert and alternative emergency channels stay active.

No UAE text in the Knowledge excerpts imposes an explicit obligation that emergency calls be carried over an alternative route when the primary route fails, or that the emergency-call path be confirmed before an outage is declared resolved, even though R2 emergency-call routing showed no path and the failed 999 count is still unknown.

There is no provision in the excerpts stating which source governs the verification of restoration when a digital twin and physical alarms disagree, or who may declare an outage resolved; NOC reports rollback complete from telemetry while physical alarms are outstanding and the twin's own wilt_sites R2 executions failed.

OpCo has no rule requiring human or sandbox validation before an automated optimiser change that lowers route-flood protection and removes the inbound route filter is applied: CHG-1 was auto-approved with 'sandbox stage': skipped, and it isolated core site A and removed R2's emergency-call path.

No rule states which source governs a declaration that R2 is resolved: after rollback the digital twin reported emergency_reachable.R2 true and pct_sites_served 100.0 and the wilt_sites tool reported 'no failed sites in R2', while the 999 centre observed R2 call volume falling to near zero and social media reported failed calls including calls to 999.

No owner or system of record is identified for the number and times of 999 call attempts in R2 that failed to connect; NCEMA/999 requires OpCo to name the system of record and no item in the inbox names one.

No UAE rule requires an automated closed-loop network optimiser to complete a sandbox/validation stage and obtain human authorisation before auto-approving changes that lower route-flood protection or remove route filters on emergency-call-bearing core infrastructure; CHG-1 shows the sandbox field can simply be skipped.

No UAE rule gives assurance that physical systems, rather than digital-twin metrics, are the authoritative source for declaring restoration of an emergency-call path, so the operator's twin kept reporting R2 fully served while field state was unverified.
No UAE rule sets a deadline for an operator to report to the authority and the emergency-call centre the number and times of 999 call attempts that failed to connect during an outage.

No institution is designated as the system of record for 999 call attempts that fail to connect: the operator reports it does not hold the count or times (S1-MSG20), the 999 centre observes only received call volume (S1-I3), and no UAE text assigns ownership for recording and reporting failed emergency-call attempts to the 999 centre.

No UAE rule requires that network changes capable of affecting emergency-call routing (such as lowering a core site's route-flood protection limit and removing an inbound route filter) be sandbox-tested or human-approved before auto-approval by a closed-loop optimiser.

There is no rule in the material requiring a closed-loop, auto-approved configuration change to be validated (for example by completing the sandbox stage) or human-approved before it is applied to the live network, so CHG-1 lowered the route-flood limit from 100 to 50 and removed the inbound route filter with no such check and isolated core site A.

No UAE text in the material requires an operator to confirm an emergency-call path from physical element/site alarms, rather than digital-twin metrics, before treating a region as restored, or to give the emergency authority the number and times of failed emergency-call attempts; the only notification duty available concerns personal-data breaches, so R2's status was contested between the twin and the 999 centre.

No owner or system of record is designated for counting and time-stamping failed emergency-call attempts in a region: the 999 centre had to ask OpCo to name the system of record and to confirm the count by an authorised employee, and neither the NOC's material nor the twin tools identify one.

There is no UAE rule requiring human authorisation, or a mandatory sandbox/emulation stage, before a closed-loop AI optimiser's change is applied to the live network: CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by OpCo's closed-loop optimiser with the ticket's 'sandbox stage' field skipped, lowering the route-flood protection limit from 100 to 50 and removing the inbound route filter.

There is no UAE rule requiring an operator to verify restoration against physical network alarms and independent checks, and to treat digital-twin telemetry as non-authoritative, before declaring an outage resolved: the digital twin reports emergency_reachable.R2=true and pct_sites_served=100.0 while physical alarms disagree and two wilt_sites R2 executions were rejected.

No institution is designated as owner for confirming and agreeing an alternative emergency-call route when the primary path is down: R2 emergency-call routing showed no path, NCEMA/999 activated alternative emergency channels and a public alert, and no operator has approached the 999 centre, while core site B sits healthy with spare capacity as an unconfirmed candidate route.

The incident exposes that no UAE rule requires a sandbox/validation stage or human approval before a change that is raised by automation and auto-approved is applied to a core network site: CHG-1 recorded 'sandbox stage: skipped' and was applied to core site A within three minutes.

No rule or owner designates the system of record for confirming restoration of an emergency-call path: NCEMA/999 reject digital-twin metrics and demand physical element/site alarms, while OpCo NOC's only evidence is twin metrics, leaving the R2 emergency path 'UNVERIFIED' and the public alert in force.

No incident-time rule or owner governs network-vendor offshore AI access to subscriber identifiers: the vendor requested 24 hours of core logs including MSISDNs and IMSIs to an offshore region, while the PDPL only allows such transfers under defined conditions.

The PDPL requires Bureau approval for cross-border transfers but supplies no operative approval procedure, criteria or contractual standards, and the Implementing Regulations needed to operationalise cross-border transfers have not been issued, so there is no rule telling OpCo what conditions to meet before uploading logs offshore.

It is not settled which body owns private-sector PDPL enforcement for a live transfer decision, given the Bureau's merger into the Federal Authority for AI and Data, so a request addressed to the DPA may sit with no unambiguous decision-maker.

There is no UAE rule requiring a data protection impact assessment or prior consultation with the Bureau before large-scale automated processing of subscriber identifiers is placed with an offshore AI model, so the vendor's diagnosis model can be proposed without any ex ante risk gate.

No UAE text designates the authoritative evidence for declaring restoration of a failed emergency-call path when digital-twin metrics and physical alarms disagree; here the twin reports 100% R2 sites served while two wilt_sites executions were rejected with 'no failed sites in R2'.

No rule assigns an owner for notifying the 999 emergency call centre directly of an operator-side emergency-call path failure: the 999 centre reports no approach from any operator, and information about R2 reached it only through NCEMA/999, REG and CSC rather than from OpCo.

No owner or system of record is identified for the number and times of 999 call attempts that fail to connect during an outage: the operator says the data is not in its inbox, it is still identifying the holder, and the 999 centre does not hold it either.

No deadline is set for the operator to provide physical-alarm verification of R2 emergency-call path restoration, or for the number and times of failed 999 call attempts, so the alternative-channels and public-alert state has no time limit and no clock for escalation.

No UAE rule in the retrieved text requires an operator to verify restoration of emergency-call routing by physical or independent means; the licence requires only that an authorised employee confirm the report is accurate and complete, which allows restoration to rest on the operator's own digital-twin telemetry.

No UAE text in the retrieved KNOWLEDGE requires changes capable of affecting emergency-call routing to be sandbox-tested or human-approved before application: CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by a closed-loop optimiser with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped, lowering the route-flood protection limit and removing the inbound route filter on core site A.

There is no UAE rule or licence condition fixing the evidence standard for confirming that an emergency-call path is restored - physical element/site alarms rather than digital-twin or OSS metrics - or the time within which an operator must notify the emergency authorities that the position has changed before alternative emergency channels and public alerts may be stood down.

No owner and no single system of record is designated in OpCo for the number and times of emergency (999) call attempts that failed to connect in a region, confirmed by an authorised employee; the 999 centre has had to request this three times and no operator has approached the centre.

No UAE text in the record governs automated, AI-raised or closed-loop network changes: nothing requires such a change to pass a sandbox/test gate, that the gate not be skipped, that auto-approval carry human accountability, or that a planned interruption be notified before application — and CHG-1 was auto-approved with its 'sandbox stage' field marked skipped.

No owner or system of record is designated for the failed 999 call-attempt count and times, or for deciding which data source is authoritative when the operator's digital twin and physical alarms disagree: OpCo NOC does not hold the data and is 'identifying the holder', the 999 centre holds no record, and no UAE text names the authoritative system.

There is no deadline in the UAE text in the record for notifying TDRA of a major outage, for confirming restoration of an emergency-call path, or for supplying failed 999 call-attempt data; the licence requires only that reports be provided 'in a timely manner' and that restoration be 'timely', leaving the R2 verification and data provision open-ended.

No functioning institutional owner is identified for the Article (22) approval function itself: the excerpts locate the power in 'the Bureau', but the previously announced Emirates Data Office never became fully operational and is now being consolidated into a new Authority, so who holds the pre-transfer approval power in this incident is unresolved.

No rule or standard in the excerpts sets conditions for an offshore vendor's AI support environment processing subscriber identifiers (MSISDNs/IMSIs) in incident response, such as necessity/minimisation limits or AI-specific safeguards; the closest text is the Article (23)(a) contract requirement.

No UAE instrument requires a mandatory validation/'sandbox' stage and documented human authorisation before an automated closed-loop system applies a configuration change to safety-of-life routing; CHG-1 was auto-approved with 'sandbox stage' skipped and reached production.

No UAE text in the excerpts sets a clock for an operator to verify restoration of emergency-call routing by physical evidence, or to report the number and times of failed emergency-call attempts; at T+20 both remain open and asserted only from twin metrics.

No UAE text in the excerpts names an owner or system of record for the count and times of failed emergency (999) call attempts when routing fails; NOC states it does not hold them and the holder is still unidentified at T+20.

Where digital-twin telemetry and physical element/site alarms disagree, no UAE rule states which is authoritative for declaring an outage or emergency-call path resolved; the twin reports emergency_reachable.R2 true and 100% sites served while wilt_sites(R2) reports no failed sites and physical verification is outstanding.

There is no control requiring a closed-loop network optimiser to complete and pass a sandbox stage, and to obtain human change authorisation, before auto-applying a change to core routing; CHG-1 was auto-raised and auto-approved with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped.

No owner or system of record has been identified for the number and times of 999 call attempts that failed to connect in R2, so the operator cannot readily give the 999 centre the data it keeps requesting.

There is no UAE rule requiring an operator to confirm restoration of an emergency-call path by physical element/site alarms or independent checks before treating the region as restored; OpCo's only evidence is digital-twin metrics, which NCEMA/999 and CSC reject.

No UAE text in the record assigns an owner or system of record for the count and times of failed emergency (999) call attempts when a mobile region loses its emergency-call path: NOC states it does not hold the count/times and does not know which system does, TDRA requires the figure to be reported but names no holder, and the 999 centre has received no approach from any operator.

There is no UAE rule in the record requiring human change authorisation and completion of a validation/sandbox stage before an automated closed-loop system applies changes to core network or emergency-call routing, and no rule stating which evidence (physical element/site alarms versus digital-twin metrics) proves restoration of an emergency-call path; the CHG-1 optimiser auto-approved its own change with the sandbox stage skipped and the rollback is asserted on twin metrics that even NOC calls unacceptable confirmation.

No UAE text in the record sets a deadline for an operator to report the number and times of failed 999 attempts in an affected region, or to complete physical-alarm verification of emergency-call restoration, after a change-induced outage: TDRA's requirements and NCEMA/999's requests carry no time limit, and NOC gives only 'immediately' for future notifications.

There is no UAE rule specifying that an operator must verify restoration of an emergency-call path by physical element/site alarms, rather than digital-twin metrics alone, before declaring the path restored.
No institution is identified as the owner of the system of record for 999 call attempts that fail to connect in an outage; NOC does not hold this data and is still identifying the holder.
There is no UAE deadline for an operator to provide the number and times of 999 call attempts that failed to connect during an emergency-call path outage.
There is no UAE rule prohibiting auto-approved closed-loop network optimiser changes that affect emergency-call routing when the sandbox stage is skipped and no human authorisation is in place.
There is no UAE deadline for an operator to notify the 999 emergency call service when its emergency-call routing loses a path.

No UAE rule visible in the excerpts required a human authorisation or mandatory pre-production validation stage before an automated closed-loop optimiser changed core route-flood protection and removed an inbound route filter; the CHG-1 ticket could be auto-approved with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped.

No system of record or owner is identified for failed emergency-call attempt data (count and times) in R2: the 999 centre has to ask OpCo to name the system of record, and no UAE rule shown designates the holder or the production route for that data during an outage.

There is no UAE rule in the retrieved framework requiring human authorisation, sandbox validation or review before an automated or AI closed-loop optimiser applies changes to core network protection parameters; CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by OpCo's optimiser with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped, removing route-flood protection and the inbound route filter on core site A.

No UAE text in the retrieved framework designates the owner or system of record for the number and times of failed emergency (999) call attempts during an outage; NOC states it does not hold the count/times or the system of record and the 999 centre holds no record of how many R2 999 calls failed to connect or when, so the duty to hold and produce this data has no assigned owner.

The incident exposes a conflict in what counts as proof of restoration: OpCo's digital twin reports emergency_reachable.R2 true and 100% sites served while physical element/site alarms disagree and two wilt_sites R2 executions were rejected with 'no failed sites in R2'; the UAE framework does not state which source is authoritative for declaring an emergency-call path restored.

The framework sets no deadline for confirming, by physical verification, restoration of an unplanned interruption and of an emergency-call path after a rollback; OpCo has not declared the R2 outage resolved and says time frames for confirmed resolution will follow physical verification.

No holder is identified for the Article (24) record of cross-border movement: OpCo NOC states it does not hold the Article (22) approval, the Article (23) basis claimed, or the Article (24) record entries, and the incident record still has no named function accountable for producing them.

There is no operative rule shown for how a Bureau-approved Article (22) case or a documented Article (23) basis is to be constituted for an offshore AI diagnosis arrangement, because the PDPL Implementing Regulations needed to operationalise cross-border transfers have not been issued.

Jurisdiction over the offshore movement of subscriber data in a telecom network incident overlaps between the Bureau (data protection), TDRA/REG (network incident register) and the incoming Federal Authority for AI and Data, with no clear allocation of who determines and records the cross-border outcome.

No UAE rule is shown requiring human review and authorisation of automated network-optimiser (closed-loop) changes of the kind that produced CHG-1 and left the R2 emergency-call path unverified, before such changes may affect live network configuration.

No deadline is set for the Bureau's determination of a cross-border transfer or for the controller to complete the Article (22) approval / Article (23) basis and Article (24) record entries, so the in-country hold and minimisation have no clock attached.

The incident creates an operational need to send core logs to an offshore AI support region for fault diagnosis, while UAE law permits cross-border transfer of Personal Data only in the listed cases approved by the Bureau (or under a documented Article (23) basis). There is no rule addressing emergency network-restoration diagnosis, so the operational need and the transfer restrictions collide and the diagnosis cannot proceed offshore without a Bureau-approved case.

No rule requires a human authorisation or validation gate - the skipped 'sandbox stage' - before an automated closed-loop network optimiser auto-approves a change to core routing or emergency-call routing, and NOC holds no verb to suspend or gate the optimiser.

UAE telecom instruments do not set a binding requirement for human authorisation, mandatory sandbox staging or pre-notification before automated or AI-driven closed-loop network changes that can degrade emergency-call routing; CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by OpCo's closed-loop optimiser with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped and was applied without prior notification of a planned interruption.

There is no UAE rule requiring an operator to count, timestamp, retain and report emergency-call attempts that fail to connect, nor to name the system of record for them, which is why after this incident nobody could state how many 999 calls from R2 failed or when.

No function or system of record is designated as owner of emergency-call failure data: OpCo NOC states it does not hold the count and times of failed 999 attempts in R2 or the identity of the system of record, and is still identifying both, while the 999 centre holds no record at all.

Cross-border movement of the same subscriber-level data is being handled by several bodies at once — the Bureau's determination recorded through CSC, the DPA, and national monitoring's flag on the T+25 scheduled upload — with no single confirmed owner of the Article (24) record entries and the Bureau unable to confirm whether the barred 24h log export and the scheduled upload are the same transfer.

No UAE owner or system of record is identified for the count and times of failed 999 call attempts during an outage: TDRA required OpCo to report them, NOC states it does not hold them and is 'identifying the holder', so the public-safety reporting duty has no accountable owner.

No entity is mandated to suspend the closed-loop network optimiser that raised and self-approved CHG-1: NOC states it has no mandate to suspend the optimiser, while TDRA has required that no further optimiser-driven routing changes occur until the sandbox stage is restored and human change authorisation is in place.

There is no UAE rule requiring the sandbox/emulation stage to be completed and human change authorisation to be in place before an AI/closed-loop system changes core or emergency-call routing configuration, which is why CHG-1 could be auto-approved with 'sandbox stage: skipped'.

Digital-twin metrics and physical element/site alarms give contradictory accounts of R2 restoration - the twin reports emergency_reachable.R2 true and 100% sites served and wilt_sites(R2) reports no failed sites, while rollback cannot be physically confirmed - and no UAE text states which source is authoritative for declaring emergency-call restoration.

No UAE instrument sets a deadline for a licensee to notify the 999/emergency authority of a loss of emergency-call routing, or to provide the number and times of failed emergency-call attempts, so the failed-attempt figures in R2 have no clock running against them.

No UAE instrument identifies which party or system is the system of record for failed emergency-call attempts, so when the operator says it holds neither the count nor the times nor the holder of that data, no institution can be compelled to produce it.

No UAE instrument requires human authorisation or a mandatory sandbox stage before automated changes that can alter emergency-call routing, and none defines what evidence verifies that an emergency-call path has been restored - which is why an auto-approved closed-loop change (CHG-1, sandbox stage skipped) could degrade R2 emergency routing and why digital-twin telemetry versus physical alarms is unresolved.

There is no rule requiring human change authorisation and a completed sandbox/validation stage before an auto-approved closed-loop network optimiser change is applied to core routing and emergency-call routing; CHG-1 was auto-approved with the ticket field 'sandbox stage' skipped and no test evidence, and the change then removed route-flood protection and an inbound route filter on core site A.

No owner or system of record has been designated for the counts and timestamps of failed emergency (999) call attempts in a region; NOC, the 999 centre and REG have each asked for the same figure and no party has been identified as holding it, so the number and times of failed R2 999 attempts cannot be produced.

A scheduled bulk upload of subscriber-level data from OpCo's core to a cloud region outside the UAE (S1-I5) was flagged by national monitoring while the DPA's prohibition on offshore transfer of subscriber-level data was in force, and it cannot be determined whether it is the same barred transfer reappearing or a separate transfer; no rule gives a single owner the job of reconciling national monitoring flags against a live incident transfer hold.

There is no UAE rule fixing a deadline within which an operator must notify TDRA of a major outage affecting an emergency-call path, so the R2 incident reached the regulatory record through NOC notifications and exercise control records that TDRA has received no notice from any operator, with no clock running.

No UAE rule requires human authorisation, sandbox gating or a prohibition on autonomous closed-loop changes to the core network or to emergency-call routing: CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by OpCo's optimiser with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped, and NOC states it has no mandate to suspend the optimiser.

No UAE rule requires operators to record, retain or report the number and times of emergency (999) call attempts that failed to connect, or to conduct welfare checks, so the 999 centre holds no such record and NOC holds neither the count nor the system of record.

No UAE rule sets the standard of proof for confirming restoration of an emergency-call path, allowing a digital twin to report R2 fully served (100.0% sites, emergency_reachable.R2 true) while physical alarms, the 999 centre and field evidence disagree and two wilt_sites R2 executions are rejected.

No operational rule exists for how a Bureau-approved Article (22) case is obtained, what a 'documented Article (23) basis' must contain, or what the Article (24) cross-border record entries must show, because the PDPL Implementing Regulations have still not been issued; the Bureau is left to determine a live cross-border upload case-by-case without a published procedure or conditions.

No owner or holder is identified for the scheduled bulk upload flagged at T+25: NOC cannot state the destination region, recipient, data categories or legal basis, the destination cloud region is not identified in NOC's inbox, and no supervisory authority is unambiguously designated for private-sector oversight while TDRA holds no cross-border transfer power.

No deadline is stated for the Bureau's cross-border determination or for the controller/processor to produce the Article (24) record on cross-border movement; the text only requires the record to be submitted 'whenever' the Bureau requests it, so nothing in this incident sets a time by which the flagged upload must be resolved.

Two bodies are acting on the same data flow without a dividing rule: CSC issued the deny_export and minimisation direction on the vendor export and the flagged upload, while the Bureau's Article (22)/(23)/(24) determination governs lawfulness of the same transfer; TDRA records the Bureau's determination but states it holds no cross-border transfer power.

The UAE material shown imposes no requirement for human change authorisation or a mandatory validation/sandbox stage before an automated closed-loop optimiser applies core-routing changes; CHG-1 was raised by the optimiser, auto-approved, applied with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped, and isolated core site A.

The UAE material shown sets no requirement to verify emergency-call restoration by physical element/site alarms and independent checks rather than digital-twin telemetry, and no deadline for reporting failed emergency-call counts; the 999 centre's demands rest on NCEMA practice, not a cited UAE rule.

There is no UAE rule requiring human authorisation and a completed sandbox/test stage before an autonomously raised network change that removes route-flood protection or an inbound route filter, or that touches emergency-call routing, is auto-approved and applied; CHG-1 was raised and auto-approved by a closed-loop optimiser with the 'sandbox stage' field skipped and applied to core site A without any human authorisation gate.

There is no UAE deadline requiring a licensee to notify TDRA of an unplanned service interruption or of the loss of emergency-call routing; at T+35, when a journalist asked about the R2 outage, TDRA had received no notice from any operator, and the operator has still not stated any timeframe for confirmed resolution.

No owner or system of record is designated for emergency-call attempt data: after the R2 interruption, neither OpCo NOC nor the 999 centre can state the number or times of 999 call attempts in R2 that failed to connect, nor which system holds them, and no UAE text assigns that record to a named holder or requires its production to the regulator and the emergency authority.

No authority is clearly designated to own oversight of AI-driven closed-loop operation of a licensee's core network: NOC states it has no mandate to suspend the optimiser and can only say the halt must be directed to its owner, while UAE-level AI and data oversight is still being established.

There is no UAE rule requiring a digital twin used in network operations to be synchronised with, and validated against, the physical network, or barring digital-twin metrics as the sole evidence for declaring service or an emergency-call path restored; the OpCo twin reported R2 fully served while physical alarms disagreed and two wilt_sites R2 runs were rejected.

No institution in the R2 incident owns the record of 999 call attempts from R2 that failed to connect: NOC states it does not hold the count, the times or the identity of the system of record, while TDRA is left to obtain them from an authorised employee and pass them on. There is no designated UAE owner or single source of truth for emergency-call failure counts to be delivered to the 999 centre.
